title: Daily count changes do not explain close pairs in two first USGS aftershock forecast sequences
abstract: We test short-time pairs in a fixed sample of 192 first USGS generic aftershock forecasts. After fixing daily counts, two of eight sequences with at least five records have excess same-day pairs separated by at most 10 minutes. Puerto Rico has 35 pairs against 13.18 expected; Nevada has three against 0.0693. Holm-adjusted Monte Carlo p values are 0.0004 and 0.0007. For Nevada, an analytic probability bound is 0.000293 for a wider null that allows separate daily rates, decay exponents from 0 to 3 and nonnegative offsets. An eight-test correction gives 0.002344. Thus daily productivity and these smooth decay changes cannot fully explain the recorded pairs under conditional independence. No test rejects after hourly counts are fixed. No spatial permutation test passes correction. Raising the magnitude threshold removes both primary rejections. These results do not identify secondary triggering as the cause and do not test later forecast updates. We provide code, a proof, aggregate evidence, simulation draws and exact source hashes. The analysis is retrospective and uses revised catalog records.
